mods.note: ﻿This index, first constructed in 2003, aggregates information on production of and investment in IT capital, employment in the information sector, and several other time series. However, due to the shift to services in the IT sector, like cloud computing and the delivery of product on non-PC platforms, the indicators became much less representative of economic activity in the sector and the series was discontinued in 2020.﻿ The latest data (updated April 13, 2020) has been converted to a FRED graph at San Francisco Tech Pulse.
Supplemental material to data files has been provided in PDF format when available.

mods.abstract: ﻿The Tech Pulse Index is an index of coincident indicators of activity in the U.S. information technology sector. It can be interpreted as a summary statistic that tracks the health of the tech sector in a timely manner. The indicators used to compute the index are investment in IT goods, consumption of personal computers and software, employment in the IT sector, as well as industrial production of and shipments by the technology sector. The index extracts the common trend that drives these series.﻿

mods.abstract: The Texas Manufacturing Outlook Survey (TMOS) is a monthly economic indicator that collects data from approximately 100 Texas manufacturers about changes in business conditions. Initiated in 2004, the survey measures changes in production, new orders, employment, prices, and company outlook, calculating indexes by subtracting the percentage of respondents reporting decreases from those reporting increases. The survey is significant for three key reasons: (1) it strongly correlates with both state-level economic measures and national economic indicators, (2) it provides data up to three weeks earlier than comparable national indicators, and (3) it offers insights into manufacturing, a sector that typically experiences economic shifts earlier and more intensely than other industries. With Texas generating 11% of the nation's manufacturing output ($296 billion in 2023) and ranking as the leading exporter of manufactured goods, TMOS serves as a valuable tool for monitoring economic trends at both regional and national levels.

﻿The Texas Service Sector Outlook Survey is a monthly assessment of service sector business conditions in Texas, providing timely economic data for a sector that accounts for 73% of Texas private-sector activity and employs over 12 million workers. Launched in January 2007 and publicly released since June 2011, the survey collects responses from approximately 230 service-providing firms about changes in key business indicators including revenue, employment, prices, and company outlook. Survey methodology involves electronically distributed questionnaires with data collection over seven business days. Results are calculated as diffusion indexes by subtracting the percentage of respondents reporting decreases from those reporting increases, with positive values indicating expansion and negative values indicating contraction. The TSSOS addresses a significant regional data gap and demonstrates high correlation with other regional economic indicators such as private service sector employment. Complete monthly results are published on the Dallas Fed website, along with collection dates and response rates.﻿

mods.abstract: ﻿The Center for Household Financial Stability and the Private Debt Project hosted three "Tipping Points" Household Debt Research Symposia, 2016-2018. All three sessions were centered on the question of “tipping points” in regard to debt: How and when does household debt move from being wealth-building and productive for households and the economy to being wealth-depleting and destructive for both?﻿

mods.note: ﻿Video of the keynote conversation "Debt-Financed Homeownership: Is it Worth the Risks? What is its Future?" featuring panelists Sarah Rosen Wartell, President, Urban Institute; Paul Willen, Senior Economist, Federal Reserve Bank of Boston; and Michael Stegman, Senior Research Fellow, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, is available on YouTube.﻿
mods.abstract: ﻿The third Tipping Points symposium, presented by the Center for Household Financial Stability and the Private Debt Project, was held in October 2018 in Washington, D.C., and looked at the evolution, impact and future of debt-financed homeownership.﻿

titleInfo.title: Tipping Points III: Debt-Financed Homeownership — Its Evolution, Impact, and Future
titleInfo.subTitle: Conference Proceedings

mods.accessCondition: For more information on rights relating to this item, please see: https://fraser.stlouisfed.org/title/tipping-points-iii-debt-financed-homeownership-evolution-impact-future-9374

mods.abstract: The second Tipping Points symposium, presented by the Center for Household Financial Stability and the Private Debt Project, was held in June 2017 in New York and focused on the macro effects of family debt.

titleInfo.title: Tipping Points II: Mapping and Understanding the Impact of Debt on Economic Growth
titleInfo.subTitle: Conference Proceedings

mods.note: The paper "Cross-Sectional Patterns of Mortgage Debt During the Housing Boom: Stocks and Flow" by Paul Willen, Chris Foote, and Lara Loewenstein was published as Federal Reserve Bank of Boston working paper 2016-12 and is available at the Federal Reserve Bank of Boston website.
mods.abstract: The first Tipping Points symposium, presented by the Center for Household Financial Stability and the Private Debt Project, was held in June 2016 in New York and focused on the micro or household-level effects of household debt.
